what_it_does: When you run software on edge devices — small computers close to where data is produced, like a smart factory sensor or a phone — you often need to predict how long a program will take to run, including when other programs are running alongside it and slowing things down. This paper introduces Pitot, a system that predicts those runtimes accurately even when you have only seen a handful of measurements, on a variety of very different hardware types, and even when multiple programs are competing for resources at the same time. It also provides mathematically guaranteed upper-bound estimates — not just a best guess, but a provable promise that the true runtime will fall below the predicted ceiling with a stated probability.
method_in_detail:
The idea. Runtime on diverse hardware is wildly variable: a microcontroller might take 1000x longer than an x86 server. And when two programs share a device, one can slow the other down by 20x. Predicting this from sparse measurements is the core challenge.

How it works. Pitot frames the problem as filling in a partially observed table (rows = programs, columns = hardware platforms, cells = runtime). The key ingredients are:

1. Log-residual objective. Runtimes span many orders of magnitude, so Pitot works in log space. It first learns a simple 'baseline' runtime as difficulty-of-program times speed-of-hardware, then trains only on the residual — how far the actual runtime deviates from that baseline in log space. This normalization makes the learning problem much better behaved.

2. Two-tower neural network. A small neural network converts program features (counts of how many times each type of instruction ran) into a compact 'embedding' vector. A separate network does the same for platform features (CPU type, memory specs). The predicted log-runtime residual is the dot product of these two vectors — similar to how recommendation systems match users to movies.

3. Interference term. When a second program runs alongside, Pitot adds a learned interaction term: it decomposes the platform's 'interference matrix' into a few interference types, each with a magnitude (how disruptive the intruder is) and a susceptibility (how sensitive the target program is). An activation function handles the case where little interference happens until a threshold is crossed.

4. Provably bounded uncertainty. Using conformalized quantile regression — a technique that wraps any predictor with a statistically valid confidence interval — Pitot produces an upper-bound prediction guaranteed to cover the true runtime at least (1-epsilon) percent of the time. A smart trick: train on multiple quantile targets and pick the one that produces the tightest bound at calibration time, without retraining.

The result. On a cluster of 24 devices ranging from a microcontroller to an x86 desktop, Pitot achieves 5.2% mean error — about 2x better than the nearest competitor — and produces uncertainty bounds that are up to 58% tighter.
